client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. I can't seem to focus at work at all — I'll be in the middle of something and then just kind of drift off, and the sadness hits me out of nowhere. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because nothing's going to bring her back.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds incredibly heavy, and those waves of sadness catching you off guard — especially at work — make a lot of sense when you're grieving someone so important to you. I also notice that even as you're sharing something so painful, there's a kind of quiet exhaustion in how you're expressing it, almost like part of you has gone very still inside. I'm wondering — beneath the doubt about whether talking will help, is there also a part of you that feels a little worn down, maybe even numb, alongside the sadness?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah... I think that's actually pretty accurate. There's this weird thing where I'll feel a sudden wave of grief, like when I saw his handwriting on an old note the other day, and then just as quickly it's like a door slams shut and I go completely flat. I don't know if that's me protecting myself or if I'm just... broken somehow.
therapist: What you're describing — that sudden rush of grief followed by everything going flat — is actually a really common and very human response to loss, not a sign that something is broken in you. Your mind is doing its best to protect you from being overwhelmed, almost like a circuit breaker that trips when the emotional current gets too strong. I'm curious, when that "door slams shut," what does that flat feeling actually feel like for you — is it more like relief, emptiness, or something else entirely?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: It's more like... emptiness, I think. Not relief, because relief would feel like something, and this is just nothing — like someone turned the volume all the way down on everything, including me. I'm still going through the motions, talking to people, eating, whatever, but it feels like I'm watching myself from a distance and none of it actually lands.
therapist: That image of the volume being turned all the way down — including on yourself — is such a vivid and honest way to describe what sounds like a kind of emotional numbness that grief can bring on, where you're present but not quite *there*. What strikes me is that even as you describe feeling nothing, there's something in your voice that carries a quiet weight to it, like the feeling isn't entirely gone — maybe just buried just beneath the surface. I'm wondering, when you say it doesn't "land" — is there anything lately, even something small, that has managed to get through, even briefly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... there was this one moment last week where I was making coffee in the morning, and the smell of it just hit me differently, and for like two seconds I thought of my dad because he always drank it black the same way I do. It was so brief, but it kind of hurt in a way that almost felt good, if that makes any sense at all. I don't know, maybe that counts, but I'm not sure if that's what you're asking about.
therapist: That absolutely counts — in fact, it sounds like something really meaningful broke through in that moment. That bittersweet feeling, where something hurts but also feels almost like a gift, is often how love makes itself known in grief — it's not emptiness at all, it's connection. I'm curious, when you noticed that feeling, did you let yourself stay with it for a moment, or did that door slam shut again quickly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I did stay with it for a little bit, actually — longer than usual, which surprised me. But then I started feeling guilty, like I didn't deserve to feel that warmth because I wasn't there enough for her when she was alive. It's like the moment I let something good in, my brain immediately punishes me for it.
therapist: That pattern you just named — where your brain swoops in to punish you the moment something good gets through — is such a clear example of how grief and guilt can become tangled together, and it's worth gently questioning that guilty voice. The fact that you *weren't* there in every moment doesn't erase the love that made that coffee smell hit you so hard in the first place. I'm wondering, if a close friend told you they felt they hadn't done enough for someone they lost, would you tell them they didn't deserve to feel warmth or comfort?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and no, I wouldn't tell a friend that they didn't deserve comfort. But it feels different when it's me, like the rules just don't apply the same way. I know that probably sounds like exactly the kind of thing you'd expect me to say, but I genuinely can't figure out how to make my brain treat myself the way I'd treat someone else.
therapist: What you just said — that you *know* the logic but can't feel it for yourself — is actually one of the most honest and important things you can recognize, and it's exactly the kind of gap that we can work with together. That double standard we hold for ourselves versus others isn't a personal failing; it's something grief and self-criticism build over time, and it can be slowly, gently dismantled. I'm curious — can you think of one specific moment, even small, where you *were* there for her, something your brain might be glossing over right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... there was this one time she called me really late, maybe two in the morning, and she was crying and didn't even really say why. I just stayed on the phone with her for like an hour, not really saying much, just being there. But my brain immediately goes to "that's the bare minimum, that doesn't count" — which I know sounds exactly like what you're talking about, but it's hard to make it feel different.
therapist: Staying on the phone in the dark for an hour with someone who is crying and can't even say why — that's not the bare minimum, that's one of the most tender things one person can do for another. And I notice that even as you're dismissing it, there's something in how you're telling it that suggests it actually meant something to you too, like part of you knows it mattered even while another part rushes to minimize it. What do you think *she* felt, in that hour, knowing you were there?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... she probably felt less alone, I guess. That's the honest answer, even if I don't fully let myself believe it mattered coming from me specifically. It's just hard to accept that my presence could actually be enough for someone when most of the time I feel like I'm this burden people have to manage.
therapist: You just gave yourself the honest answer — she felt less alone — and that's not a small thing, that's actually everything when someone is crying at 2am. But I want to gently stay with what you said at the end, because it feels important: this sense that you're a burden people have to manage sounds like it goes deeper than grief over your grandmother, like it might be something you've been carrying for a long time. I'm wondering, where do you think that belief about yourself first came from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... yeah, it probably does go back further than just losing my grandma. I think it started when I was pretty young, like my parents were always so stressed and busy, and I learned pretty quickly that having feelings or needing things just made everything harder for everyone. So I kind of internalized this idea that the best version of me was the one who didn't take up too much space.
therapist: What you just described — a child learning to shrink themselves to keep the peace — is such a heavy thing to have carried quietly for so long, and it makes so much sense that it would shape how you see yourself now. The way you're speaking about it feels very calm on the surface, but I get the sense this is actually quite tender for you, like you've learned to talk about even painful things in a way that doesn't take up too much space — which is exactly what that little kid was taught to do. I'm wondering, what would it feel like to let this one actually land, to let it matter, right here?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know... when you put it that way, something kind of tightens in my chest, like I want to brush past it the way I always do. It's weird because I've told this story before, to other people, and it never felt like much, but right now it actually feels kind of... real, I guess. I'm not sure I know how to just let something matter without immediately telling myself I'm being too sensitive or making a big deal out of nothing.
therapist: That tightening in your chest — that's not you being too sensitive, that's actually the feeling of something true making contact. The fact that this feels different from other times you've told this story might be because right now you're not just recounting it, you're actually *in* it, and that takes real courage. Can you just stay with that tightness for a moment, without rushing to explain it away — what is it telling you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
